title: GAME THREAD: Washington meets up with Kansas State
description: Good morning, Cougar football fans. Your Washington State Cougars are getting ready for Week 2 non-conference action against the Kansas State Wildcats. WSU is coming off a narrow loss at rival Washington on Sunday, 24-10. Despite the loss, the Cougars had plenty of positives to take away from the Apple Cup. Mainly, from the defensive […]
fullText:
Good morning, Cougar football fans.

Your Washington State Cougars are getting ready for Week 2 non-conference action against the Kansas State Wildcats.

WSU is coming off a narrow loss at rival Washington on Sunday, 24-10. Despite the loss, the Cougars had plenty of positives to take away from the Apple Cup. Mainly, from the defensive side of things. The Cougar defense held Washington to just 10 points through the first three quarters and 2-10 on third-down conversions. It wasn't until Washington's final two drives that they really began to stack up the yards and explosive plays. In a game that WSU was three-possession underdogs in, they were within a score at multiple points in the final quarter. The front seven is what stood out for WSU in that game, containing the Huskies' run attack and putting pressure on quarterback Demond Williams Jr. Offensively, the Cougars have room for improvement. They will likely be without speedster wide receiver Tony Freeman, who suffered an injury in Week 1. Caden Pinnick showed flashes of brilliance last time out, scampering for 61 yards and a touchdown, and seemed to settle in later in the game with his arm.

Kansas State cruised through Week 1, defeating FCS Nicholls State 71-3. Quarterback Avery Johnson threw for 199 yards and three touchdowns before coming out of the game midway through the third quarter. Six different Wildcats ran in touchdowns in the game, with junior Rodney Fields Jr. leading the way with 101 yards on 14 carries and one of those six touchdowns.

Kickoff is set for 9 a.m. PST and will be broadcasted nationally on TNT and streaming on HBO Max.

title: This Long-Awaited Feature Is Finally Coming to the Apple Watch
description: Apple has finally figured out we want to know our step count.
fullText:
We expect fitness wearables to count our steps—an idea that Fitbit borrowed from pedometers forever ago. In recent years even Oura and Whoop have added step tracking. But the Apple Watch has never made it easy to see your step count, even though it’s been keeping track in the background all along. Apple is finally changing that.

On the product pages for the Series 12 and the Apple Watch Ultra, Apple boasts that the new watches give you a more accurate step count—interesting, because step count hasn’t been a selling point in the past. And then comes the big news: “And now you can more easily check your step count, right from your watch face.”

So far, it has been frustratingly difficult to get a step count on your watch. You would think you could easily add that number to a watch complication (a complication being a mini data field for the watch face), but nope—if you want a little counter of your steps on the watch face, you have to install a third-party app to provide that.

I kind of understand why: Apple wanted to set itself apart from the Fitbits of the world. You’re supposed to close your rings, and rings are based on movement, exercise, and stand hours. I can imagine somebody at Apple saying “no, step counting is dumb” and they were arguably right. But the idea has stuck in the public consciousness; we now expect step counts, and Apple is finally going to deliver.

First of all, the Apple Watch already counts your steps. You can see your step count by going to the Health app on your phone and searching for Steps. Scroll to the bottom of the Steps screen and tap Add to Pinned. Now it will be the first thing you see when you open the Health app. (Surprised the Health app can do this? You have no idea of the hidden gems in that thing.)

To get a step count on your Apple Watch right now, without upgrading anything, you’ll need to install a step counter app. Duffy is a popular (free) one; there are plenty of others out there, so choose one you like. These apps typically provide a complication, so you can add your step count to your favorite watch face.

But what about taking advantage of Apple’s new embrace of the step count? Apple says the feature will be available on the Series 12 and Ultra 4 watches. That said, this seems like a very simple software change, so I’d bet money that step count will become available in WatchOS 27, which is due out any day now, and which will run on Series 9 and newer, Ultra 2 and newer, and the SE 3. I’m currently using the WatchOS 27 public beta, and there’s no step count feature yet, but I’m watching for it.

I also spied step counts in Apple’s screenshots of its upcoming redesign of the Health app. This is an app that lives on your phone, and in the screenshot there was a little tile with your Apple Watch rings, and underneath the rings, the step count. Apple says the Health app redesign will be available on devices that support Apple Intelligence, which means the iPhone 15 Pro and newer.

Once you have the feature on your watch, it looks like step counts will be available on the cards you see when you swipe up from the main watch face. Currently you can pin a card there with your step distance for the day (I’ve covered 0.65 miles between waking up and making my way to my home office) but steps aren’t available there yet.

title: Yes, the Apple Watch's New Audio Intelligence Features Really Are Always Listening to You
description: If you think that sounds like a privacy nightmare, you're not wrong.
fullText:
During its Sept. 9 keynote, Apple announced the Apple Watch Series 12 and the Ultra 4, both of which will come with a feature that passively listens to your audio conversations all day and can summarize them for you on demand. It's part of a collection of features called "Audio Intelligence," but the two key features to consider here are:

Live Rewind: If you double-press the Digital Crown on your Apple Watch, it will pull up a text snippet of your conversation over the last fifteen seconds.

Siri Recaps: Your watch listens to your conversations and generates an AI summary of any of your transcribed audio at the end of each day.

At first glance, the basic concept seems like a privacy nightmare, but Apple has put some safeguards in place to help people feel more comfortable with this feature: The audio that is captured is never recorded or stored, and never leaves your device; it is essentially deleted immediately and in real time from local storage; only a truncated version is uploaded to Apple Private Cloud Compute servers for AI processing, and the resulting transcript that is delivered to you is end-to-end encrypted.

Still, there are some potential privacy concerns worth considering, especially since you'll essentially be subjecting everyone around you to using it without their consent.

Series 12 and Ultra 4 watches run on an S11 chip with a Secure Exclave feature, a partitioned local storage compartment that even the operating system cannot access. When your Apple Watch picks up ambient audio, it is sent straight into this protected buffer, where it is encrypted, then sent over to a matching Secure Enclave on your paired iPhone.

From there, your iPhone transcribes it locally using an on-device AI model to create a summarized version that’s half the length of the actual audio, removing everything but the essentials, and stripping out any identifying information. After the audio data is overwritten, the transcript is sent to Apple's Private Cloud Compute along with some generic metadata, like a rough location and timestamps.

None of the audio data is tied to your Apple ID once it reaches the servers at this stage. Apple uses a third-party relay to conceal your IP address while uploading the data to Private Cloud Compute, so not even their employees can identify you from your device. While in the Private Cloud Compute servers, your audio data gets summarized by Siri AI. This is how you end up with daily text summaries of your audio, provided you opt into Siri Recap. Siri Recap summaries are auto-deleted every seven days unless you choose to save them individually.

All of this might seem perfectly secure, but here comes the risky part: If you choose to save a conversation summary with Siri Recap, that data is uploaded to your iCloud storage and can even be saved in apps like Apple Notes or Journal. Server-level data breaches at companies like Apple are rare, but account-level hacks happen more often than you might think: 900,000 compromised iCloud logins were found sitting on a public server after a data leak just this January.

If someone manages to hack into your Apple ID or access your unsecured iPhone, they might be able to view all your saved conversation summaries from a single place. And it’s not just the potential data breach that should scare you, but all the associated privacy concerns.

Apple has spent a lot of time thinking through ways to protect its customers when they use the Audio Intelligence feature, but none of these protections extend to other people who might be sitting across the table or in the same room as you.

To its credit, Apple has added an audio chime and a brief visual cue that plays on your watch whenever the Live Rewind feature is triggered. This is intended to inform people around you that they are being listened to. Live Rewind also doesn’t identify speakers, so it won’t name or otherwise identify the person speaking in the transcriptions or summaries—but none of that actually prevents people from being eavesdropped on without their explicit consent.

Siri Recap’s implementation is arguably even worse. It has no audio or visual cues to indicate that it’s running, so no one knows that they are being surveilled if you enable this feature. Apple’s privacy documentation is visibly scarce when it comes to the issue of consent, apart from a vague warning on the product pages that advises you to “be mindful of those around you.”

This is a potential concern not just for other people who might worry about being spied on every time they see an Apple Watch, but also Apple Watch users themselves, if they are in a region where local laws require consent before recording audio: Some 12 U.S. states have explicit all-party consent laws that forbid undisclosed recordings, while outside the U.S., many E.U. countries have instituted similar requirements; the E.U.'s GDPR also prohibits recordings containing personally identifiable information without disclosure.

Using an Apple Watch with the Audio Intelligence feature enabled might sound like it would put you in violation of these laws, but at this point, it seems the device operates in a bit of a grey area—as Apple's privacy documentation notes:

Audio Intelligence features do not create audio recordings that can be accessedby the operating system, apps, the user, or Apple. There is no recording to share,forward, or produce if requested by any party, because no recording exists.

The Secure Exclave buffer where the audio is initially processed is "a continuously overwritten stream that exists only within the protected hardware and never creates an audio recording," Apple says, meaning no one needs to consent to being recorded. In theory. But that Apple felt the need to go into great detail to explain how the feature technically doesn't violate any privacy laws probably doesn't make it feel any less dystopian to those inclined to view it that way.

Given all the potential security concerns, it’s a good thing that Apple has at least made its Audio Intelligence features opt-in only. They won’t be enabled by default on your new Apple Watch, and you can choose to enable or disable individual features as you choose to. Here's what to look for:

Sound Recognition: Open the Settings app on your iPhone. Navigate to Accessibility > Sound & Name Recognition > Sound Recognition. Here you can toggle the “Detect using Apple Watch” option on or off.

Music Recognition: Open the Settings app directly on your Apple Watch. Tap on Smart Stack. Switch "Music Detection" on or off per your needs.

Live Rewind: Open the Watch app on your iPhone. Go to Siri > Live Rewind. You can choose to enable or disable “Double Click Digital Crown” to control this feature.

Siri Recap: Again on the Watch app on your iPhone, go to Siri > Siri Recap. You can enable or disable the feature here, or even set an autorun schedule for it if you like. Siri Recap can also be switched on and off by flipping a single toggle in your Control Center.

title: How the iPhone Duo Stacks Up to the Pixel 11 Pro Fold and Galaxy Z Fold 8
description: How does Apple's new foldable compare to the rest?
fullText:
After years of rumors, Apple finally made a foldable: the iPhone Duo. The initial reaction online has been mostly positive—particularly how iOS adapts to the phone and that cool transition wallpaper effect—but it begs the question: How does Apple's new device compare to the folding phones already on the market?

The iPhone Duo is now competing against the Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold and the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 (which I'll focus on here rather than the Z Fold 8 Ultra). There are key similarities and differences between the three handsets that suggest whether or not the iPhone Duo will be a success. And having used both Google and Samsung foldables in the past, I have some ideas about what the iPhone Duo needs to get right.

Google and Samsung have been doing this longer than Apple has, and their phones are thinner and lighter than the iPhone Duo. That might make a difference once Apple's handset gets out into the world, with preorders set to start on Friday, Oct. 16. You can also see here that Apple and Samsung have gone for the "passport" style approach: Displays that are shorter and wider, which means a more tablet-style main display. The Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold has the aspect ratio of a standard smartphone when closed, with a main display that's more square.

You can see how the passport-style foldable compares to the more traditional foldable form factor in the display dimensions too: There's a lot more vertical space on the Pixel 11 Pro Fold when all of these foldables are closed shut, which is quite a consideration. If you're like me, you'll end up using your foldable closed more often than unfolded, in which case the outer display becomes very important. (But more on that later.) It's worth knowing that both Apple and Google rely on Samsung to supply their phone displays, as per industry sources.

If you'd like a foldable phone, it's going to cost you, whichever brand you favor. The iPhone Duo starts a little higher than the competition and goes up to 2TB of storage—something Google and Samsung don't do. It's worth mentioning RAM here too: The iPhone Duo has 12GB, the Google phone comes with 16GB, and Samsung offers either 12GB or 16GB in the Galaxy Z Fold 8, depending on the amount of storage you buy. But it's not an even comparison: The Duo runs iOS, which has different RAM requirements than Android devices.

Cameras abound on foldable phones—you need a selfie camera for the inner display and the outer display—and it's notable that Apple isn't telling anyone the specs of its inner selfie cameras. Google's foldable is the only one with a telephoto camera. In the modern era, software processing is just as important as hardware specs, so how the handsets compare on this front is to some extent subjective. It'll be interesting to see how photos from the iPhone Duo stand up against those on the iPhone 18 Pro, which has a more advanced camera system.

The iPhone Duo doesn't have face unlock as the Google and Samsung phones do, and the Galaxy Z Fold 8 doesn't have the IP68 waterproofing of the iPhone Duo and Pixel 11 Pro Fold (though this doesn't last). Battery life is a key consideration when picking a smartphone, but the capacity numbers here can only tell us so much. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold has a 4,806 mAh battery, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 has a 4,800 mAh battery, and Apple isn't revealing the battery capacity on the iPhone Duo—though it does say you can get up to 44 hours of video playback between charges on the outer display. Software optimization and other factors play a role too, so some real-world testing will be needed for a proper comparison.

Speaking of software, there's the iOS and Android divide, of course. From what we've seen of iOS on the iPhone Duo, it looks like an elegant and thoughtful adaptation, with shifting buttons, split keyboards, a dual pane mode, and some other nice touches—no doubt helped by Apple's iPad experience. To my eye, it seems like a more fluid experience than what you get on an Android foldable, though that's not to say you get a bad experience on Google and Samsung phones.

Spec sheets can only get you so far, and while the iPhone Duo has made a bold impression based on what we've seen from Apple so far, no one has properly used one yet. The true test for whether the foldable iPhone is a hit or not is going to depend on how well it works through all the moments of day-to-day life.

I've spent several years using foldable phones from Samsung and Google, and aside from the rather prohibitive cost, the main issue that makes me still prefer standard phone form factors is that, for most of the time, there's no reason to open up the full display—which means you're left with a device that's chunky and heavy, with no real upside. Checking messages on the go, making contactless payments, taking photos: the majority of phone tasks don't need or suit a tablet-sized screen. That's what all of these foldables are fighting against. Would you use an iPad to take a photo at a gig, call your parents, or find your way around in an unfamiliar city?

Apple seems to have the software experience right, and the iPhone Duo looks as well crafted as you would expect a foldable iPhone to be—but even if you can foot the bill for one of these, you might find that the cost of using a thicker, heavier, smaller phone isn't worth it, just so you can occasionally have a bigger screen available. The iPhone Duo actually stacks up pretty well against the foldables from Samsung and Google, but its real competition is going to come from other iPhones.

title: You Don't Need the Apple Watch 12 to Get All the New Health Features
description: Some features require the newest Apple Watch, but others will work on the watch or phone you already have.
fullText:
Apple recently announced some big changes to the Health app, as well as new sensors in the upcoming Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. The company bundled these and other health-related announcements together, but that doesn't mean you need an Apple Watch 12 to take advantage of all the new features. Here's the breakdown of which Apple Watches will get the new features—and which ones don't need an Apple Watch at all.

You'll need the new Series 12 or the Ultra 4 to get Apple's new heart rate sensor—the one it's billing as the most accurate in any wearable. (Huge if true.) These two watches also have the new S11 processing chip. The sensor and the chip are required for what Apple is calling its "health sensing system," which gives you more frequent heart rate and HRV readings throughout the day.

According to Apple, the new systems measure heart rate every five seconds instead of every five minutes, and HRV every five minutes instead of every few hours. Overnight vitals will now include a Recovery HRV score that's compared to your baseline (so you know when your body is under more or less stress than usual). The Readiness score seems to rely on these readings, so you'll need one of the new watches to get that score.

I recently wrote about the changes Apple has planned for the new Health app and noted that those are likely to be software changes that don't require a new phone or watch. Apple writes in a footnote on the Apple Watch page that the redesigned Health app requires an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone (or iPad). The full list of Apple Intelligence-enabled devices is here, and they include the iPhone 15 Pro and all iPhones 16 and newer.

The new app includes "insights," which seem to be similar to the trends you'll see in the current Apple Health app. If you've ever noticed the little cards that say things like "your cardio fitness has been trending up for 8 weeks," it seems we'll get more of those, and they'll be collected together into their own area of the app. There will also be text summaries of your data and recommendations for what to do next, apparently written by Apple Intelligence based on your data.

The new Health app includes an on-demand VO2max test you can do indoors. Apple's event video showed a person propping up their phone on the floor, making sure the phone's camera could see their entire body, and then following along with a metronome by stepping in place on the beat. You'll need a heart rate sensor to do this test and get your results, and Apple says that any Apple Watch will do—or AirPods Pro 3, or a third-party sensor.

In other words, it sounds like it can work with any device that broadcasts heart rate, which includes just about any wearable out there. If you have a Fitbit, a Whoop, or a Garmin (to name a few), you can probably get it to broadcast your heart rate and thus work with this test. Apple's Fitness app can already read heart rate from these devices, so I expect the compatibility to be the same for the VO2max test.

Workout Buddy, which takes the form of a motivational voice in your ear during workouts, requires Apple Intelligence. Previously, this meant you needed to carry an Apple Intelligence-enabled phone with you during workouts, but that's changing. The new Workout Buddy can work from your Apple Watch without needing a phone, so long as your watch has access to the Internet through either cellular data or a wifi network (such as your gym's wifi). Compatible watches include the Series 9 and newer, the Ultra 2 and later, or the Apple Watch SE 3.

title: The hinge for Apple's new foldable phone was built with AI
description: Apple says it used AI and 3D printing in the manufacturing process for its long-awaited foldable phone.
fullText:
Duo, Apple’s long-awaited foldable phone announced at the company’s Surprise and Shine event on Wednesday, contains a number of surprises, including a critical hinge that was designed and built with the help of AI and 3D printing.

The new phone represents Apple’s first entry into the foldable phone genre — a category of devices that has seen significant consumer enthusiasm but whose form factors haven’t always lived up to the hype. As you might expect from a product that, by design, undergoes twice as much wear as a traditional device, most foldables suffer significant degradation and don’t have the durability of other smartphones.

Apple claims that it has integrated innovative protections into the Duo’s design to keep the phone from falling prey to the typical wear and tear associated with foldables. That includes the hinge, according to Johny Srouji, the company’s chief hardware officer.

“During manufacturing, we use AI algorithms to precisely match each individual hinge with its best-fit housing to ensure perfect alignment, and a confocal laser progressively scans the topology of every single unit and 3D prints up to 25 micro layers of a custom photopolymer to eliminate residual waviness,” Srouji said during Wednesday’s event.

Srouji also shared that Apple gave the foldable phone “a custom nano-texture finish that significantly reduces glare and reflections,” as well as a multilayer lamination strategy designed to increase the device’s durability. Of course, it remains to be seen whether those protections will be enough to keep the Duo in peak physical condition in the long run.

title: Six Ways the iPhone Duo Has an Edge Over Android Foldables
description: Though late to the party, Apple's first foldable brings a lot of innovative design to the table.
fullText:
I've followed the foldable smartphone space for seven years now, but I’ve still never wanted to buy one. But the iPhone Duo is making me doubt my convictions, and not just because I’m an iPhone user. Until now, foldable smartphones felt like a work in progress to me, requiring a sacrifice or two (or three) with either the hardware or the software.

But with the launch of the iPhone Duo, it feels like this everything is finally coming together. Apple's hardware and the software appear to be working hand in hand to provide a seamless, and even fun, foldable experience. It still feels like choosing the Duo instead carries its own share of compromises—missing Face ID, no telephoto lens, and the lack of an Action button)—but what the new device brings to the table might make up for all of that.

It’s a trick, but it’s surprising no one thought of this before. When you open the iPhone Duo, the cover screen performs a blurred animation that seamlessly continues to the inner screen. What’s on the cover screen appears on the right side of the inner screen. The interface also adapts to the hinge and the degree of folding. Make it a tent, and it shows the Stand By widgets. When watching media, you can prop it up like a laptop, and the interface splits in two as well, with the top half showing the media, and controls on the bottom half (assuming the app has been optimized to do so, anyway). If you’re playing a game or watching a movie on the inner screen, closing the Duo will switch the content to the cover screen, with the animation, and without skipping a beat. This is the kind of seamless device/software integration that's tough for Android devices to compete with.

Apple is late to the foldable party, but at least it has caught up in the screen and hinge tech. Of course, we won’t know exactly how creaseless it is until we can all get our hands on the iPhone Duo, but based on the coverage so far, it is at least fairly creaseless. In day-to-day use, you might not even notice it.

More interesting is the inner display tech: Apple is bringing a version of the nano-texture display from the MacBook Pro line to this device. The matte display fights reflections, but it also hides the crease—something that’s harder to do with the glossy panels sported by Android foldables.

As noted, the real hardware-software advantage shows up in how iOS works. Because of the shorter display, Apple has chosen to dedicate the right-hand side edge to the Dock and toolbar controls, an interesting choice in terms of reachability and design.

The usable space isn’t compromised, either with the cover screen or the inner display. Adapting and moving the toolbar, and bringing third-party apps along for the ride, is no easy feat. It’s also something that would be extremely difficult to pull off on the Android side: It would require a design directive from Google, and manufacturers would have to find their own ways to implement it.

It will be interesting to see how third-party developers adapt to the new screen and layout options. Apple already showcased how media apps like Netflix are taking advantage of the split-screen interface design. Zoom’s example, where the screen sharing is on one side and the meeting participants are on the other, is quite smart, too.

How you end up using the inner screen on a foldable is all down to how developers take advantage of it. Sure, you can put two apps side by side, but how often are people really going to do that? But the fact that you have an iPad mini-sized canvas, along with upcoming support for the Apple Pencil, sets the stage for creative uses of the expanding display. Conversely, Samsungdropped support for its stylus from the Fold series last year.

Under-display selfie cameras are not new—Samsung tried it in Fold 3, and gave up in the Fold 7. The under-display camera just wasn’t as good. This is the first time that Apple is trying it, and we will have to test it out before we can make a judgment on how well it performs.

But that's not the only camera-related feature in the iPhone Duo. While it's missing a telephoto lens, the way Apple is using the second screen in the camera and FaceTime is very interesting. When you're photographing someone with the Duo unfolded, the cover screen becomes a live preview, so the subjects can see themselves, and guide you as well. To make it easier to capture moments with kids, the outer camera can show fun Snoopy graphics. Even FaceTime has a Duo mode where a participant can be shown on the cover screen.

Most foldable smartphones lose out when it comes to dust and water resistance. The design itself means you have to be careful with dust, especially around the hinges. The Samsung Fold 8, for example, has an IP48 rating. The iPhone Duo gets the full IP68 sealing treatment. An IP68 rating means that the iPhone Duo is fully dust-protected, and it can survive under shallow 1.5 meter deep water for 30 minutes. The Samsung Galaxy Fold 8 lacks a dust-sealing rating, though it does offer stronger water resistance.

All that new tech does come at a cost. The first is literal: the $1,999 starting price, or more than buying an iPhone and an iPad mini combined. The foldable design ushers in a new era of iPhone innovation, but it’s also leaving behind features that iPhone users have come to love and expect. There’s no Face ID, no Action button, no real optical zoom, and no physical SIM card slot, all lacking in a device that’s quite heavy (254 g) compared to the iPhone 18 Pro (211 grams). Ultimately, the market (and buyers' wallets) will decide if these tradeoffs are worth it, but if you ask me, the Duo makes the most compelling case for a foldable yet. 

iPhone Duo pre-orders open October 16, and the device won’t ship until October 23.

title: If You Love 'Dark Matter,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next
description: If you’re looking for alternate versions of Apple TV’s sci-fi hit, try this trippy 2014 movie.
fullText:
Apple TV sure has the touch when it comes to high-concept sci-fi thrillers that get into your head and won't leave. Based on the book by Blake Crouch, Dark Matter is a near-perfect speculative thriller-mystery, packed with twists and turns and brought to life by an absolutely stacked cast.

This story of parallel universes and parallel selves who don’t always have their (or your—it’s confusing) best interests at heart is addictive. If the weekly release schedule is giving you the shakes and you’ve already burned through our list of the best streamalike series, then there’s one movie that’s a perfect match: 2014's Coherence.

If you love the sense of paranoid danger that suffuses Dark Matter, you’ll love Coherence, which explores similar themes. And if you thought the idea of a parallel version of yourself trying to steal your life was cool, imagine multiple parallel versions of yourself sowing chaos over the course of a few hours, until you have to take extreme measures to protect yourself in a world where you suddenly can’t be sure if your friends are really your friends.

The story is set on the night of an “astronomical anomaly” in the form of a comet passing very close to Earth. Eight friends with complex histories gather for a dinner party. Just as their personal dramas start to derail the evening, the comet comes to its closest point, the power goes out, and things get weird. One house in the distance still has power, but when two of the group walk there, they discover it’s the same house they just left—except not. And when they return, carrying a strange box filled with personal items and photographs of everyone with a number written on the back, everyone knows they’re in for a long night.

It slowly becomes clear that there are multiple realities overlapping, and the dinner guests from other universes have also gone out exploring—and now they may all be mixed up. And not all the parallel people are to be trusted. The tension keeps rising as mysterious blackmail notes, violent attacks, and impersonations abound, leading to a shocking ending composed of nested twists. Whether you love the way Dark Matter handles Jason’s desperate attempts to hang onto his real family, the idea that you can’t trust what you see, or the twisty sci-fi stuff at the show’s core, you’ll love Coherence for all the same reasons. Stream Coherence on Kanopy, Tubi, Hoopla, or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

Anyone who loves a show about multiple realities wants multiple movie options. If you need a few more recommendations for movies with Dark Matter’s atmosphere of dread and wild twists, here you go.

If it’s the exploration of the concept behind parallel universes and doppelgangers that excites you, this film’s more thoughtful, quieter mood is perfect. The same day that an Earth-like planet is discovered, 17-year-old Rhoda (Brit Marling) accidentally kills a young boy and his pregnant mother. Her life falls to pieces, and when she leaves prison, she seeks out the woman’s husband, but can’t bring herself to confess her identity. She enters a contest to be one of the first civilians to visit Earth 2, which is revealed to be a mirror world where everyone has led roughly—but not always exactly—the same lives. The revelation leads to an emotionally powerful ending that will resonate with fans of the show. Rent Another Earth on Prime Video.

Is it the way Dark Matter’s Jasons work against each other that you find so compelling? Check out The Double, based on a short novel by Fyodor Dostoyevsky. Jesse Eisenberg plays Simon James, a timid man who is ignored by almost everyone in his life. One day, a man named James Simon begins working in his office—a man who looks exactly like him, but who is confident, outgoing, and cruel. The twisting story of how James impacts Simon’s life is unexpected, thoroughly entertaining, and perfectly pitched for Dark Matter fans. Stream The Double on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

The question of what you would do if you could access parallel dimensions is the engine that drives Dark Matter deep into your brain—and it’s the same one that powers Parallel. title: Apple Just Announced the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max
description: Apple's latest "Pro" iPhones are official.
fullText:
The iPhone Duo will inevitably steal tech headlines this week. After all, Apple finally made a foldable iPhone to compete with options from Samsung and Google. But while an iPhone with two displays is novel and exciting, it's also going to be expensive. I imagine there are many in the market for a new iPhone who aren't interested in spending as much as $2,000. There are also likely customers who don't want a foldable iPhone, and would prefer the standard smartphone design they're used to. That's where the iPhone 18 Pro comes in.

If you have an iPhone 17 Pro, you might confuse it for the iPhone 18 Pro. Indeed, Apple hasn't changed the overall design much this year, which is to be expected. The iPhone 17 Pro refreshed the Pro iPhone design with its large camera bump and plane of glass for MagSafe charging. The 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max aren't much different—though now the metal is color-matched to the back glass.

That being said, there are some changes here you may notice upon closer examination. Perhaps first you'd notice the 18 Pro's Dynamic Island is smaller than it has been on previous Pro iPhones. With it, you're able to run three tasks at once, rather than two. That may prove useful depending on what you're doing, or it may end up cluttering the top of your iPhone. 18 Pro users will have to be the judge. You'd also notice some new color options not available on the iPhone 17 Pro, which I'll cover below.

The displays will remain the same sizes as last year—6.3 inches on the iPhone 18 Pro, and 6.9 inches on the iPhone 18 Pro Max. But now, these displays use a more efficient LPTO+ technology.

Like the iPhone Duo, the iPhone 18 Pros come with Apple's new A20 Pro chip built on 2nm technology. The company touts how the new chip is great for processing AI on-device, with a six-core CPU, seven-core GPU, new Neural Accelerators, and a second Neural Engine. Apple focused on the A20 Pro's thermal cooling with the new vapor chamber in the 18 Pro. Apple says this means there are significant sustained performance improvements over the iPhone 17 Pro.

Apple says this chip has the fastest CPU in a smartphone, with 50% better memory bandwidth. But, as with all performance claims, we'll have to wait until testers try out the A20 Pro for themselves. Still, Apple's newest chips always improve on the previous generation by some degree, so it's safe to say the 18 Pro (and the Duo at that) will be the fastest iPhones yet.

Apple also says the iPhone 18 Pro has 36 hours of battery life while streaming video, while iPhone 18 Pro Max has 45 hours. The company says five minutes of charging gets you six hours of video playback.

Perhaps the biggest change for the iPhone 18 Pro this year is its cameras. Apple's Pro iPhones are known for their shooters, but for the 18 Pros, Apple has taken things up a notch. For the first time, these iPhones have variable apertures. When using the 48MP main camera, your iPhone can physically open and close its aperture to control how much light hits the sensor—up to 50% more light than before. That offers two benefits: In dim environments, you can let in more light than you normally could. You can also use the aperture to control the depth of field, or the background blur. A large aperture (more light) means a blurrier background, while a smaller aperture (less light) means a cleaner background.

Apple also introduced Pro Controls, which has been sorely missing on the iPhone. You now can control white balance and shutter speed, and check the histogram. This mode works for both photography and videography. There's now a new "smart focus tracking" feature that uses AI to keep focus on a subject. Photographic Styles get some additional upgrades and controls, and Time-Lapse also supports 4K. With the 18 Pro, Apple is rolling out a "reference" feature to ensure that an original shot can be confirmed if an edit is later made with AI. Apple calls this a "digital negative."

As previously mentioned, the iPhone 18 Pro's colors may be one of the most recognisably "new" features of this generation. Apple is rolling out color options in "Burgundy," "Glacier," and Silver, though the first two may be the more distinct of the bunch. Still, it's more variation than we have on the Duo.

Everything is getting more expensive, thanks to RAMaggedon, and the iPhone 18 Pro is no exception. Apple is raising the starting price this year to $1,199 for the 256GB model, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299 for the 256GB variant.

Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro will be available to preorder on Saturday, Sept. 12 at 12 a.m. PT (3 a.m. ET). The devices then go on sale Friday, Sept. 18.

title: Where’s the iPhone 18?
description: Apple is giving its iPhone release schedule the biggest shake-up in history.
fullText:
There was something different about today's "Surprise and Shine" launch event from Apple: We didn't get the unveiling of the iPhone 18.

For the first time since Apple started releasing multiple iPhones per year, which was 2013 with the arrival of the iPhone 5c and the iPhone 5s (simpler times), we have several pro-level handsets without the standard version to accompany them. So what's behind the shift? And is the iPhone 18 canceled? Apple, predictably, isn't saying, but we've got enough clues to make an informed guess.

If you've been keeping up with Apple rumors since the launch of the iPhone 17, you'll know that this has long been predicted—notably by the most respected purveyor of Apple leaks in the business, reporter Mark Gurman. Gurman was predicting in Bloomberg as far back as November 2025 that we would only get the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the folding iPhone Duo in 2026.

The reason? According to Gurman, it's to spread out revenue more evenly across the year, rather than having most of the iPhones unveiled every September. It also takes some of the pressure off Apple's marketing teams and reduces the likelihood of mishaps like that Siri AI upgrade—which was announced way before it was ready. Gurman also went on record as saying that this is likely to be the norm for "years to come," so get used to it.

However, Gurman wasn't the first to break the news. In May of 2025, Wayne Ma at The Information reported that Apple would hold the standard iPhone 18 model over until 2027, based on conversations with anonymous supply chain sources. As per that report, one of the motivations behind the shift was to make more space for the folding iPhone, which makes sense considering it's Apple's first attempt at the form factor.

Just a day later, well-known and usually well-informed Apple analyst Ming-Chi Kuo backed up the story, saying that we'd see the foldable iPhone, the iPhone 18 Pro, the iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the iPhone Air 2 (then called the iPhone 18 Slim) in September 2026. Apart from that last handset, he was right.

Kuo added an extra reason for the shift as well: Competition from phone manufacturers based in Asia. A lot of these manufacturers release their flagship handsets during the first half of the year, including Samsung, and as far as Apple is concerned, that can leave it playing catch-up by the time September rolls around.

While the iPhone 18 was a no-show at the "Surprise and Shine" event, there's no indication that it's been canceled. Apple still wants to cater to those who'd rather spend a little less on their iPhones (the iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,119), and the most educated guesses we've seen suggest we'll get the base version of the phone sometime in March.

It's unlikely to be on its own either. We're also expecting to see the iPhone 18e and the iPhone Air 2 appear at the same time, following on from the iPhone 17e (launched in March 2026) and the original iPhone Air (launched in September 2025, alongside the iPhone 17 series).

And that "e" phone series set the foundation for the calendar shift we've now seen with the standard iPhone 18 model. The first of these more affordable handsets, the iPhone SE, showed up in March 2016—it was then followed by the iPhone SE 2 (April 2020), the iPhone SE 3 (March 2022), and the iPhone 16e (February 2025). That shows Apple has been eyeing up the February-March-April slot for non-pro-level iPhones for a decade at this point.

The rumors so far suggest the iPhone 18 will use an A20 chipset, while we're likely to get a RAM bump as well. We now know that the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max have a smaller Dynamic Island, with the ability to show up to three Live Activities, and that's something that should carry across to the standard model (along with iOS 27).

Apple didn't mention the iPhone 18 at all today—not even in a post-credits sequence—but it would be a major surprise if the handset didn't make a belated appearance sometime in the first quarter of next year. If this is the iPhone that's for you, you're just going to have to wait a little while longer.

title: Apple Just Announced the Foldable 'iPhone Duo'
description: It's Apple's first foldable smartphone.
fullText:
Since Apple announced the date of its big September event, we've expected the company to reveal the "iPhone Ultra," its first foldable smartphone. As it turns out, half of that prediction came true: While the company did indeed showcase the first iPhone to transform from smartphone to tablet, it isn't actually called the Ultra. Instead, the company surprised us all with a new name: iPhone Duo.

It's immediately apparent that the iPhone Duo has a much different design than any iPhone Apple has ever made. This device is foldable, which means it has two functioning displays, depending on how you use it. When closed, the Duo has a funkier 5.4-inch display than the one you might be used to on an iPhone, but it's fully functional. You don't actually have to open up the Duo to use it: You can text, browse Safari, play games, and do whatever you normally would on your iPhone from here. The selfie cam and two rear cameras mean you can take FaceTime calls and shoot photos and videos while the Duo is in this position. If you never wanted to open up your Duo, you would probably never have to.

Open it up, however, and you'll be greeted by a much larger 7.6-inch display. This is the benefit of foldable smartphones: You have access to a mini tablet (sometimes called a "phablet") whenever you want it. That extra screen real estate means you can view single apps in a much larger window, but also run two apps side-by-side. That's a first for any iPhone, even if it's not a first for smartphones in general. And because this is a tablet-like display, your Home Screen looks a bit more like an iPad's, complete with extra widgets and a macOS-like Dock. There's even a Dock on the outer display, and many controls are adjusted to sit on the right of the display to make them accessible using your thumb.

Interestingly, the Duo is the first iPhone in years to lack Face ID. Instead, this device marks the return of Touch ID, integrated into the Side button. (You can also unlock it with your Apple Watch.) It also supports Apple Pencil for the first time on iPhone, and includes two batteries, providing 31 hours of video playback on the inner display, and 44 hours on the outer. You can reach 50% battery in 20 minutes of charging, and five hours of use after five minutes.

It works in many different orientations: You can stand it up tent-style or like a laptop, or fold it slightly to split your keyboard. It also works in StandBy by folding it on its side.

Like the iPhone 18 Pros, the iPhone Duo comes with Apple's new A20 Pro chip. But for the Duo, the chip has a new display engine to power both screens. Apple says it offers up to 35% faster performance than iPhone 17 Pro. While I'm sure it's Apple's fastest chip yet, we'll have to wait until independent benchmarkers put it to the test to know how much better it is than the A19 Pro. The Duo also has Apple's proprietary C2 modem, which provides faster uploads and quicker reconnection to networks.

As noted above, the iPhone Duo has four cameras: two rear cameras and two selfie cameras. Let's start with those rear cameras: Apple has a 48MP fusion lens and a 2x telephoto lens. Some might be sad about the omission of an ultrawide lens. At the same time, the Duo might not be the iPhone for users who care most about mobile photography. Perhaps it'll feel more like the cameras on the iPad: useful to have, but not exactly a selling point. Like the 18 Pro, the Duo supports 4K Time-Lapses and new Photographic Styles.

Perhaps more importantly, the Duo has two selfie cameras: one on the front display, and one on the inner display. This ensures that you can take FaceTime calls and selfies in whichever orientation you have the iPhone Duo in. Crucially, the inner camera is embedded in the display, so you don't ever see it. There are a lot of camera perks with those dual displays: Your subject can see themselves in the outer display; you can stand up the Duo like a tripod; and you can project FaceTime calls on both displays, so everyone can see who you're talking to.

Apple didn't go all out with the colors for the Duo. Buyers will only have two options to choose from here: Star White or Night Sky (dark blue). That's in contrast to the iPhone 18 Pro, which comes in four interesting colors. That said, I'm guessing Apple doesn't expect Duo sales to be affected by color options: Buyers are either going to pay up for the Duo, or they're not, and fun colors probably wouldn't play into that conversation.

Apple's first foldable iPhone doesn't come cheap, of course. The iPhone Duo officially starts at $1,999, which makes this the most expensive iPhone Apple has ever made. And yet, that doesn't sound so bad: Initial reports suggested that the Duo would be more than $2,000, which seemed quite believable considering how RAMaggedon is driving the costs up for all types of tech.

The iPhone Duo can be more expensive, however. $1,999 is the starting price for the 256GB model, though it goes up to 2TB.

While Apple announced the iPhone Duo today, it won't be available right away. Instead, the company says preorders begin Oct. 16, while sales begin Oct. 23. While iPhone preorders are usually a frantic affair, I imagine the Duo's demand will be historic. If you're interested in picking one up as soon as possible, you'll likely want to make sure you preorder it as soon as Apple lets you.

title: Apple's 'Reference Image' Preserves Your Original Photos (Even After You Edit Them)
description: You can think of it like a permanenet digital photo negative.
fullText:
Figuring out what’s real online is only getting harder, and AI watermarks can only go so far to identify fakes. But today, Apple introduced a new standard to at least help identify real images taken directly on an iPhone: Apple Reference Image. It won’t solve the problem of finding the truth online, but it could be a helpful tool towards that goal.

The new feature will be available on iPhone 18 Pro models to start. It works by taking signed sensor data from the camera and using it to create a reference picture that can’t be edited, alongside a version that can be changed. The idea here is to give you a version of the picture that’s authenticated at the moment of capture, which you can compare against any modified versions later.

This provenance metadata can be preserved through certain supported sharing methods, which for now means select other Apple devices can check their verification status. That doesn’t mean that anyone can check the veracity of an image—especially if the version that gets posted and shared is an edited variant—but it provides a tool for the person or organization that took the picture originally to offer proof of verification.

This tool comes alongside the announcement that Apple will soon add support for the SynthID standard. This will potentially help users identify when an image has been created or modified with AI. Apple joins a long (though not exactly comprehensive) list of major tech companies to support the standard, including OpenAI, Nvidia, and obviously Google, the original creator of SynthID.

We’re still in the midst of a scattershot image verification ecosystem. Apple’s Reference Image is a clever implementation that gives the end user a signed original to compare a picture against, which is a step up from C2PA metadata that merely embeds information about an image’s origin. It’s still unclear how widely these verification tools will be implemented and how easy it will be for users to trace where an image comes from and how, precisely, it was modified, but still, something is better than nothing.

title: Why the Apple Health App's Redesign Is a Big Deal
description: We've needed this dashboard for years.
fullText:
Apple announced new watches today—a Series 12 and an Ultra 4—which you can read more about here. But alongside the watch features, Apple announced a revamped Health app. We’ll soon have a proper dashboard for health data and insights, rivaling what you can get from the companion apps for other wearables like Whoop, Garmin, and Fitbit.

Apple was an early trendsetter when it came to health-focused watches, but it quickly fell behind as all the other devices began adding sleep scores, recovery scores, and customized insights based on your day’s data. If you open up a good wearable app, you’ll instantly know what’s going on with your body’s data and what you should probably do about it. I’m often skeptical of the specifics—you shouldn’t read too much into any app’s metrics—but it’s good to have something to look at.

The Apple Health app has existed for years, but it’s mostly a dry listing of data from different sources. Which is a shame, because it has access to an incredible amount of data, not to mention powerful hidden features that most of us never manage to discover.

Last year, Apple finally revamped its Fitness app to match what other wearables give us in terms of activity tracking. This year, we finally get the other half: a Health app that can tell you how well you slept, how “recovered” you are, and how your long-term health seems to be shaping up.

Although Apple showed these features in the context of an Apple Watch upgrade (more on that below), the things that intrigue me most are likely to be software updates that roll out to iPhones in general. That’s my guess, in any case—I’ll watch Apple’s announcements 

Apple showed a new Readiness score, which can tell you whether you need to “recover,” should “pace yourself,” are “ready,” or should “go for it.” (That’s in order from worst to best.) This score can update during the day, making it a more readable version of something like Garmin’s Body Battery.

When you open your Health app, it looks like relevant “insights” will show up at the top of the screen, including your sleep, recovery, and rings, and the main screen can show your sleep from the past night along with a sleep score. The app includes text summaries and guidance that are generated by Apple Intelligence, suggesting that you'll need an iPhone 16 or later for these.

In the screenshots Apple shared, I spied a tiny number that is actually a huge change of focus for the company: one of the insights shows your rings next to your step count for the day. Apple has never made a big deal about steps, to the point where people often download third-party step counters to be able to easily view steps on the watch. But the Health app has kept count all along, and now that number is showing up somewhere you can easily see it.

Depending on how well Apple executes this idea, I could see apps like Bevel becoming obsolete. And Bevel already makes some wearables’ apps (like Google Health) obsolete—you can just read the data from Bevel, or now Apple Health, instead of using the app that comes with your Fitbit. Other fitness tech companies will now have a serious competitor that is available for free on customers’ phones.

I roll my eyes every time a health or fitness app claims to gauge my “longevity” or some true “age” of my body. Depending on which app you ask, I’m either 10 years younger than I really am, or three years older.

Apple has joined the club, with a whole Longevity tab in the Health app. (That now brings the number of tabs to three: the main screen, the sharing tab, and now longevity in the middle.) Despite the eye-rolling, I see what Apple is doing here. Don’t think of longevity in this (or any) app as being an accurate gauge of how long you will live; think of it as how your long-term health habits are adding up. Apple’s longevity calculations involve seven areas, with icons indicating something like nutrition, exercise, heart health, hearing health, movement (maybe steps), sleep, and mental well-being.

There’s also a new set of assessments, including a VO2max assessment. According to Apple’s presentation, you’ll prop your phone up where it can see your full body, and then you’ll step to a metronome’s beat, speeding up as the beeps speed up until you’re running in place. This sounds like it may have been inspired by the Harvard step test, which has you step up and down in place and then measure your heart rate. Until now, Apple’s VO2max estimates have always been based on GPS-tracked activities like outdoor running. (Apple finished in the middle of the pack when I tested the accuracy of nine devices’ VO2max estimates. I’m curious to see whether the new assessment does better.)

When it comes to the full experience—with the Apple Watch itself—there’s a notable upgrade to the Series 12 Apple Watch compared to previous versions. Apple has redesigned the heart rate sensor on the back of the watch, with larger lights and redesigned photodiodes to detect the reflected light.

With these redesigns, Apple says it has the “most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable.” To which I say: I’ll believe it when I see it. In my testing over the past few years, Apple Watches have lagged well behind other wearables’ heart rate sensors when I test them for accuracy. I’d certainly believe that it found room for improvement, but is the new Apple sensor really going to be able to beat Garmin’s fifth-generation sensor, the one that made me do a double take because I thought I had it mixed up with my chest strap data?

Apple has released a whitepaper with the results of an internal heart rate accuracy study it did comparing the Series 12 (but not the Ultra 4) against the Garmin Forerunner 970, Google Pixel Watch 4, Huawei Watch 5, Samsung Galaxy Watch 8, Whoop 5.0, and Oura Ring 5, with a Polar H10 chest strap for reference. It's a short paper, and doesn't show the kind of detail I would like to see from a thorough test, so you can bet I'll be investigating this myself once I get my hands on the new watch. If Apple really reaches a Forerunner 970 level of accuracy, I’ll be incredibly impressed.

fullText:
The new model will serve as the first big test for John Ternus, who took the role last week

All eyes are on Apple’s annual fall announcement of new products this afternoon, where the company is expected to unveil the most significant change to the iPhone since the smartphone’s introduction in 2007.

Unlike previous iterations, the new iPhone is expected to fold, opening and closing like a passport to double its screen size.

The product release event, titled “Surprise and Shine”, begins at 10am Pacific Standard Time on Apple’s campus in Cupertino, California, south of San Francisco.

While competitors have released foldable smartphones since the late 2010s, the new model will be a first for the iPhone maker and will also serve as the first big test for the company’s new CEO, John Ternus, who assumed the role on 1 September.

Apple is expected to price the phone north of $2000, more than what some of its competitors charge for their foldable phones. A Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold, for instance, retails for $1899. Much remains unknown about Apple’s device, including its name, though it is rumored to be named either the iPhone Fold or the iPhone Ultra.

Apple reportedly began testing prototypes of its folding iPhone display in early 2021 – though at the time there were no plans for its launch, according to a Bloomberg report. Ultimately, the phone the company is rumored to launch will be about 5.5in when it’s closed and 7.8in when it opens. It’s also not expected to have Face ID because the device is too thin to hold the camera that would enable the facial recognition scan. Reports indicate it will only offer Touch ID instead.

Apple is also expected to make several more routine announcements, including new iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max models. Though the foldable iPhone may take center stage Wednesday, demand for foldable phones makes up only a small sliver of overall mobile device sales. Customers’ interest in standard iPhones, by contrast, remains high, as evidenced in Apple’s most recent robust earnings.

The company is also expected to unveil new iterations of some of its other product offerings at its events and over the next few months, including updates to its Apple Watch and AirPods lines, according to Bloomberg, as well as its first-ever touchscreen MacBook.

Ternus will take the stage as CEO for the first time and mark the beginning of his tenure as the head of Apple, replacing outgoing CEO Tim Cook. In a note to employees on his first day, Ternus said that he was excited about “the incredible products already in the works and the ones we haven’t even imagined”.

“I’m honored to be stepping into this role at what is truly the greatest company in the world, and I am so excited about everything we have in store,” Ternus wrote in his letter. “We have a huge launch next week that’s going to be phenomenal. Thanks for everything you’ve all done to make it possible.”

fullText:
Lisa Nandy says government will introduce legislation after talks end without breakthrough

Apple and Google will be forced to block explicit images on children’s smartphones by law in the UK after talks failed to produce a breakthrough, the government has said.

The legislation commitment puts ministers on a collision course with two of the biggest players in Silicon Valley, months after the government announced a social media ban for under-16s.

Lisa Nandy, the secretary of state for digital, culture, media and sport, said the government would start work on an act of parliament to stop under-18s taking, sharing or viewing nude images on their devices.

Talks with Google and Apple, whose operating systems dominate the smartphone market, had not reached agreement as a three-month deadline passed on Tuesday.

Nandy told the House of Commons the tech companies could still reach a deal but it was “almost certain” groundbreaking legislation would be required.

“For too long, technology companies have failed to protect children from some of the worst harms,” she said. “And to be frank, I am not prepared to give them the benefit of the doubt that progress will continue at the pace that we need it to, while harm is being done now.”

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said the protections would be “built into the device and switched on by default”, and tech companies will be required to verify an adult user’s age before they are allowed to take, view or send nude images. The government also wants the restrictions to apply to apps used by children, which will require further legislation.

Nandy said: “This will ensure that the whole ecosystem changes, tackling the means by which children are most often abused or groomed in the online world.”

Sources familiar with progress in the talks have said there iwas a desire to reach a deal on both sides but significant hurdles remained including privacy concerns on the tech side.

Jess Phillips, the Labour MP and former safeguarding minister, said the legislation would stop the UK from producing self-generated child sexual abuse material, where children are duped or groomed into sharing explicit images of themselves.

However, she urged the government to ensure the UK was followed by other countries and to make sure that “while we lead the world, we’re not standing alone for too long”.

Hannah Swirsky, head of policy at the Internet Watch Foundation, which monitors the online spread of child sexual abuse material [CSAM], said: “It is deeply disappointing that tech firms have failed to act in full, but we are pleased that the government is now taking decisive legislative action to keep children safe.”

Last year the IWF said a quarter of the images or videos of CSAM it recorded were self-generated, representing more than 140,000 pieces of content over a 12-month period.

One of Keir Starmer’s final acts as prime minister was to give Apple and Google three months to stop under-18s from generating, sending or seeing nude images on their devices, by activating built-in features on the hardware or other technological solutions. Between them, Apple’s iOS and Google’s Android smartphone operating systems dominate the mobile phone market.

The nudity block implies the use of “client-side scanning”, where content is scanned by software on the device before it is encrypted or sent.

“Client-side scanning is the least evil approach,” said Lukasz Olejnik, a visiting senior research fellow in cybersecurity and privacy at Kings College London. “That said, it does put in place an infrastructure to scan content of messages.”

Privacy campaigners have also warned that adults would have to verify their age before switching off any nudity-blocking features. In June, the government said the proposals would “not affect the use of devices owned and used by adults who verify their age”.

Google said it was “pleased to have made progress” in talks with the government and was “fully committed” to working with legislators, experts, app developers and device manufacturers to “keep children safe, while also protecting privacy and access to information”.

An Apple spokesperson said the company was preparing to strengthen its “communication safety” feature, which warns children when they are receiving or sending nude images and videos.

“We share the UK’s commitment to combating exploitation and abuse online, and have shared with UK officials future plans to strengthen communication safety and other tools even further to help keep kids safe.”

Apple iPod Engraver (2019)
description: Making the iPod engraver page for Apple’s online store
fullText:
I spent 2004–2006 working at Apple as a UI engineer for their online store. Part of my job was to prototype concepts that would add some interactive sparkle to the site.

One such project improved the “Personalize your iPod” page, where customers could submit two lines of text to be engraved on the back of the iPod they were ordering.

As originally designed the page offered no interaction beyond a plain form. I added a rotatable iPod, a live “engraved” preview of the customer’s text, and a highlight of any change in shipping times.

I animated the iPod by cycling through a series of JPEGs using JavaScript. The engraving was created using imagemagick, which took the user’s text and returned an “engraved” image to be overlaid on the rear of the iPod. The shipping highlight was achieved by switching CSS classes to change the background color, in the style of a classic yellow fade.

There’s an old working demo if you’d like to try it yourself.

We obviously have much better ways of doing such things today, but in 2005, with limited browser technology, those solutions seemed a little bit magical.

title: Kimi K3 (2.8T) at 1 token/s on a MacBook Pro, streamed from four SSDs
description: ARGODRIVE Deltafin: Kimi K3 (2.8T MoE) streamed from SSDs on Apple Silicon — fork of gavamedia/deltafin with the ARGODRIVE storage work and benchmark package - argonautlabsai/deltafin
fullText:
A fork of gavamedia/deltafin (MIT) running Kimi K3 from SSDs on Apple Silicon, with the ARGODRIVE storage work. The benchmark package, placement manifests and results are in k3-public-bench/; the measurement instruments are published separately as ARGODRIVE. Credits and what this fork changes: CREDITS.md. The upstream README follows.

Deltafin is a single native binary that runs full Kimi K3. Nothing pruned. Nothing skipped. K3 decides every token.

All 16 experts, every single token. No shortcuts, no "close enough." It's exactly what Moonshot shipped.

The quality rule is simple: K3 itself decides every token, and nobody else. Small draft models are allowed to guess ahead (that's where much of the speed comes from), but K3 checks every guess, and nothing reaches you without its official sign-off.

Pure raw uncut K3 quality, as fast as possible. Speed must never come from reducing model quality. Deltafin keeps all 16 routed experts and the full K3 target as the sole authority for every single token.

Our goal is to squeeze out every last drop of efficiency possible when running a huge model like K3, with all options on the table... except for reducing quality.

Deltafin is not a product pitch. It is an experiment in how far consumer hardware can be pushed, and what we can learn by attempting something so challenging.

Kimi K3 targets infrastructure on the scale of 16 nodes and roughly 4.8 TB of aggregate VRAM. That means the full 2.8T parameters and the 1M-token context window, with the expert bank never pruned. On any home setup, this is an extreme constraint. Every 1% improvement is very hard-won. But each gain can teach something.

Research and exploration is the point. That is our mission. Not everything has to be a "minimum viable product" to impress venture capitalists. If Deltafin helps make frontier models usable on a $15,000 home setup, instead of a $2,000,000 infrastructure like Kimi recommends, we believe that is worthwhile progress on our self-hosted AI journey. Plus everything learned along the way could even benefit other projects in unexpected ways.

“We choose to run the full 2.8-trillion-parameter model locally, and do the other things, not because they are easy, but because they are hard.”
— John F. Kennedy probably

Other projects appear to run full K3, somehow faster. But look closer: they've re-encoded K3's expert bank down to ~3 bits. Clever engineering toward a different goal: the smallest K3 that fits and is "close enough." Those weights are no longer the ones Moonshot released, and nobody, including them, has measured what those compromises cost.

Deltafin is the other experiment: every expert byte exactly as Moonshot shipped it, made as fast as physics allows.

Deltafin installs almost everything it needs. See Requirements if you're missing anything.

Or, if you don't have enough disk space:

setup --stream installs the resident model and fetches exact experts on-demand only, initially running far more slowly when routes have no local cache yet. As you build up your cache over time, this can be a way to save space, storing only the parts of the model you use, running entirely off cache on disk.

The normal setup includes Inferact's Kimi-K3-DSpark. It takes 6.635 GiB on disk and approximately 4.49 GiB when admitted at runtime. Deltafin avoids materializing DSpark's redundant copy of K3's embedding. Chat and server requests use DSpark automatically when beneficial; any failures, insufficient headroom, or bad live economics simply leaves full K3 running by itself.

Qwen is a separate add-on for faster raw text continuation:

Qwen speeds up raw completion only: the small models guess what comes next, K3 checks the guess, and you get identical output in less time. That helps code autocomplete and other /v1/completions traffic, plus deltafin run --prompt ... — one measured 17-token completion ran 2.7× faster with the same output IDs.

This adds 4.337 GiB on disk, and because Qwen will not improve chat speed, we make it an optional add-on. You can add it to a fresh install with deltafin setup --full --include-qwen, or add it later with the command above.

upgrade gets what you need, and rebuilds the binary. Models, converted weights, and caches are left alone. It never re-runs setup or re-downloads K3.

Continue only when git status --short is empty. If it lists files, preserve or commit that work yourself, rather than allowing an upgrade procedure to guess. Existing model data remains in the same repository-root directories.

upgrade needs a clean, non-diverged branch, and it remembers how the binary was built, so an NVIDIA/CUDA build stays a CUDA build rather than quietly falling back to CPU. Anything unexpected safely stops the upgrade.

upgrade ignores build environment variables — it reuses whatever the binary was already built with. So to switch configuration (CPU to CUDA, say, or a moved LibTorch tree), run cargo build --locked --release yourself once with the new variables set; see Requirements. That becomes the recorded setup, and later upgrades keep it.

Without --stats, generated text streams normally instead of printing one diagnostic line per token. --max-new N limits new tokens; it does not alter the prompt or context. Chat output stops at K3's control boundary, while raw completion should normally use a bound.

Long conversations are far slower than short completions — prefill and cache grow with history, and startup prints the actual usable context bound.

The native server implements /v1/chat/completions, /v1/completions and /v1/models, including server-sent-event streaming. Point an OpenAI-compatible client at http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1 and use any non-empty local API key expected by that client.

The server implements a deliberately small, strictly-checked subset of the OpenAI API — text-only, one generation at a time, always greedy and reproducible — and refuses anything it cannot honor exactly with a normal OpenAI-shaped error instead of silently ignoring it. Growing chats automatically benefit from exact conversation-state reuse, draft-verified DSpark speedups and an exact-response memo; every accepted field, refusal rule and caching detail is in the server reference.

The default server response ceiling is one million tokens. Lower it with --max-tokens N when integrating clients, and raise client timeouts because full K3 responses are slow. Request JSON is bounded by --max-request-bytes (128 MiB by default). Keep the server on loopback unless you add your own authentication and network boundary.

Deltafin exists because other people published amazing work:

Exact provenance and distribution boundaries are recorded in Third-party provenance and notices.

Deltafin's tracked project code is MIT. Kimi K3 weights, the DSpark checkpoint, optional Qwen checkpoints and all other third-party material retain their upstream terms. Deltafin is an independent project with no affiliation to Moonshot AI.

title: Five Devices I Expect Apple to Announce on Wednesday
description: Apple will announce its first-ever foldable iPhone tomorrow.
fullText:
Apple has a big event scheduled for tomorrow. On Wednesday, Sept. 9, at 1 p.m. ET, the company will take the virtual stage to announce a series of new products. Exactly what those products are, only Apple knows for sure. But thanks to leaks and rumors, we generally know what some of those updates are going to be. I'm confident we'll see these five devices announced tomorrow, though Apple may have other updates in store for us as well.

The defining product announcement for Apple tomorrow will be the iPhone Ultra. The Ultra is Apple's first foldable iPhone, undeniably the biggest update to the iPhone line in years (or, perhaps, ever). Like other foldables, the iPhone Ultra will feature a "smaller" display when closed (perhaps 5.5 inches), and will open to reveal a larger display within (rumors suggest 7.8 inches). Leaks suggest the devices will have two rear cameras in addition to a selfie cam, though it may use Touch ID rather than Face ID.

Apple will likely debut its new A20 chip with all its new iPhones this year, Ultra included. The company may pack in 12GB of RAM and a larger battery to accommodate the dual displays—perhaps 5,000 mAh or 5,500, per the rumors. While we won't know for sure until we see it, leaks suggest Apple has managed to reduce the appearance of the Ultra's "crease," or where the display folds in. If so, the Ultra could have one of the better-looking foldable displays on the market, but, again, we won't know until tomorrow.

While most of the iPhone Ultra's specs are exciting, one thing is anything but: its price. A foldable iPhone was always doomed to be expensive, but thanks to the ongoing memory crisis, all tech is pricier than ever. Rumors suggest the iPhone Ultra will start at more than $2,000. As of this article, Apple's most expensive iPhone is the $2,000 2TB iPhone 17 Pro Max, but even it has a starting price of $1,199 for 256GB.

Apple isn't doing away with its traditional iPhone design. On the contrary, the other iPhones Apple is expected to announce tomorrow, the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, will be small updates from last year's iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max. (As an owner of the latter, I'm happy I don't have much pressure to upgrade.)

Here's what's new from last year: According to the rumors, the iPhone 18 Pro line may ship with slightly smaller Dynamic Islands than before. While you'll still see the camera cutout, it won't be quite as prominent as on the iPhone 17 Pro series, which gives you a bit more screen real estate to work with. In addition, the new devices may get cameras with variable apertures, as opposed to the fixed apertures in the 17 Pros. That would allow the 18 Pros to take in more light in dark environments, like how many traditional cameras work. Like the iPhone Ultra, the iPhone 18 Pros will likely get the A20 chip, so unless Apple has made any major breakthroughs here, expect the usual slight increase in performance and efficiency. The 18 Pro could also ship with Apple's C2 modem, which may offer more privacy benefits in addition to cellular performance.

Rumors also suggest the 18 Pro and 19 Pro Max batteries could be larger and more efficient, but since Apple is private about its battery specs, we'll have to wait for independent teardown videos to know for sure. What most of us will be happy to see, however, are the new colors. While the 18 Pro should look almost identical to the 17 Pro, you'll have color choices like dark cherry and sky blue, and likely at least one more option: either black, light gray, or both. Like the Ultra, the 18 Pro will likely cost more than ever this year. The base model may ship at $1,299, while the 18 Pro Max may start at $1,399. Once you start bumping up the storage, the price may only increase.

That's it for iPhones, at least if the rumors can be believed. Apple may push other iPhones, like the iPhone 18, 18e, and iPhone Air 2, into the spring of 2027, but if they do, it isn't clear whether they'll punt the entire announcement or simply share that these phones will be available next year. (My money's on the latter.)

Apple's next-generation Apple Watch is likely coming tomorrow, too. The Apple Watch Series 12 might not change much from the Series 11, but rumors point to three key updates. First, as expected, there's a new "S-series" chip, the S11. While there isn't much out there on performance, it will be Apple's first Apple Watch chip released during its big AI push, so, presumably, it will help power some of those new features. Turning to health, the Series 12 may bring an "always-on" heart-rate sensor, similar to what you can find from WHOOP, which could give you more health data than the current watches.

Finally, Apple may bring back the ceramic watch option this year in two colors: white and dark gray. We don't have much pricing info yet, but when Apple released the ceramic Series 5, it started at $1,299, so that option could get quite expensive in our RAMaggedon era.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is also light on rumors. From what I see, leakers expect an Ultra that looks much like the Ultra 3, with similar upgrades to the Series 12. That means the S12 chip and an always-on heart-rate sensor. While I expect to see the Ultra 4 tomorrow, I don't expect it to be an overhauled device.

While the above five products are almost guaranteed to debut tomorrow, other devices aren't so locked in. As MacRumors highlights, Apple has some other products in the works that may or may not make it to its big September event. They include a new Apple TV 4K with an upgraded chip, a new HomePod mini with a faster processor, and, most notably, the "Home hub," which would be Apple's first smart-home display. That device could come with a seven-inch screen, a camera, motion sensors, and more, capable of running Siri AI, making video calls, and streaming content. Apple could also release fifth-generation AirPods with the H3 chip, but we'll have to wait until tomorrow to know for sure.

Apple will also likely take tomorrow to confirm release dates for its upcoming slate of software updates, including iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27 Golden Gate, and watchOS 27. If you have a compatible iPhone, iPad, Mac, or Apple Watch, you'll be able to install the updates for free whenever Apple drops them.
